lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Rebuilt weekly carrier scorecards used by 6 regional managers to renegotiate contracts, cutting late deliveries from 11% to 7% in two quarters.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites; my redesign of the slotting rules was rolled out with the floor supervisors and 45 retrained pickers.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing, Python
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: Make the résumé’s target and the transition to the diesel mechanic role clearer.
items.because: The move from an MBA and product internship to that role may prompt questions from product or operations employers.

items.says: Keep date formatting consistent across entries.
Adjust the emphasis for the target role.
items.because: Product applications should give Harbor Payments and the product project the most attention, while operations applications should foreground Crestline results.

items.says: Make sure the profile link is complete, clickable, and points to the intended profile.
Keep the contact line compact.
Add a strong MBA focus, distinction, or credential if it is relevant and meaningful.
Clarify whether under five days is an average, a target, or true of every job.
items.because: The measurement is hard to interpret.

items.says: Give a comparison or context for the dry-dock time if available.
Clarify the connection between the maintained systems and the harbor authority’s inspections.
Add a substantiated compliance, reliability, or inspection outcome.
items.because: Without one, the bullet is less compelling than the first.

items.says: Specify what the 2,300 figure represents.
Clarify what the 9-to-4-day comparison is against.
items.because: The comparison needs enough context to be credible.

items.says: State the conversion change in percentage points.
items.because: The metric moves from 61% to 66%.

items.says: Clarify whether the 40,000 figure refers to sessions or unique users.
Clarify whether the test result was statistically reliable.
Be precise about the scope of “all merchants.”
Explain or validate support tickets as the RICE Reach measure.
items.because: It is an unusual proxy for the number of users or scope of an opportunity.

items.says: Reduce the list of activities and make the decision or outcome more prominent.
items.because: The bullet describes research and analysis but does not say what priority was selected.

items.says: Avoid repeating the preceding bullet’s roadmap-prioritization point.
The test and conversion result repeat the prior checkout bullet.
Check that the reported customer effect matches the test’s randomization unit.
items.because: Session-level randomization and customer-level interpretation are not automatically equivalent.

items.says: The onboarding result repeats an earlier bullet.
Avoid repeating the earlier roadmap work.
Clarify whether the two-region rollout was approved, funded, or completed.
items.because: The wording should not imply implementation if only funding was secured.

items.says: Explain how the scorecard work contributed to fewer late deliveries.
items.because: The causal link is asserted but not explained.

items.says: Clarify the period or comparison behind the 11%-to-7% result.
Specify the measurement period or baseline for the 30% reduction if available.
Clarify your role in the rollout and the pickers’ retraining.
items.because: It is unclear whether you personally trained the 45 pickers or coordinated their retraining.

items.says: Define “forecast error” consistently if the audience may interpret it differently.
Separate or prioritize the tool, SOP, training, and negotiation contributions.
items.because: The combined activities make the key result harder to follow.

items.says: Clarify how the 1,800 annual driver hours were measured.
Clarify whether the driver-hour saving was realized or estimated.
Clarify whether the nine tonnes is an actual measured amount.
Define “first year.”
Make your role in the launch clearer.
items.because: The result should not be attributed only to the app or dining halls.

items.says: The weekly-active-user growth calculation is wrong.
items.because: Going from 400 to 1,150 is a 187.5% increase, not 150%.

items.says: Avoid implying the interviews alone caused the usage increase.
items.because: They should support the reminder-feature design decision.

items.says: The fill-rate change is stated as 20% rather than 20 percentage points.
items.because: It moves from 75% to 95%.

items.says: Add a timeframe for the fill-rate result if available.
Distinguish your contribution from other changes if possible.
Make clear that the $2.4M annual saving is modeled or projected.
items.because: It is not a realized saving.

items.says: Replace the passive framing with a clear account of your contribution.
Say what changed and what benefit followed, with a measurable outcome if one exists.
items.because: The bullet does not currently give that result.

items.says: Clarify whether this approval is the same pilot decision reported in the savings bullet.
items.because: If it is the same, the approval is reported twice; otherwise, the two decisions need distinguishing.

items.says: Support broad product skills such as roadmapping and user interviews with experience bullets.
items.because: They are more persuasive when backed by experience.

items.says: Categorize Python consistently rather than placing it under “Product.”
items.because: Python is a technical skill.

items.says: Give a Python proficiency level or specific use if useful and accurate.
Specify Excel capabilities if they materially strengthen the application.
